# A worked example: one paper, end to end {.unnumbered}

The book has taught the parts. This appendix assembles them into one short paper on the running heart-failure cohort, so you can see the moves in place rather than in isolation. Read the paper first. The notes afterwards point each choice back to the chapter that explains it.

::: {.callout-note}
## About the worked data

The cohort here is simulated, on purpose. A textbook needs a dataset it can publish in full, regenerate on demand, and design to show a specific teaching point; no real patient dataset can be all three. [`figures/sw_cohort.py`](https://github.com/tiagojct/working-draft/blob/main/figures/sw_cohort.py) draws 5,204 fictional patients from a fixed seed, so every number below is reproducible and every figure regenerates from code ([reproducibility](reproducibility.qmd)). The findings are invented but clinically plausible. Treat the paper as a model of *form*, not a source of evidence.
:::

## The paper

**NT-proBNP at discharge and 30-day readmission after acute heart failure: a retrospective cohort study**

**Abstract.** **Background.** Thirty-day readmission after heart-failure hospitalisation affects roughly one in five patients and is often preventable; risk stratification at discharge remains imperfect. **Objective.** To assess whether N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide (NT-proBNP) at discharge predicts 30-day unplanned readmission. **Methods.** In a retrospective cohort of 5,204 adults discharged after acute heart failure, NT-proBNP was measured within 24 hours before discharge. Thirty-day unplanned readmission was ascertained from the national registry. Multivariable models were adjusted for age, sex, LVEF, and NYHA class. **Results.** The readmission rate was 12.8% (95% CI 11.9–13.7). Higher discharge NT-proBNP was independently associated with readmission (adjusted OR 1.25 per log-unit, 95% CI 1.14–1.38, p < 0.001). **Conclusion.** Discharge NT-proBNP identifies patients at higher 30-day readmission risk and may support targeted follow-up.

**Introduction.** Heart failure accounts for more than a million hospital admissions a year in Europe, and readmission within 30 days is common and costly. Whether a single discharge biomarker adds usable prognostic information beyond routine variables is unsettled. We asked whether NT-proBNP measured at discharge predicts 30-day unplanned readmission in adults hospitalised for acute heart failure.

**Methods.** We studied a retrospective cohort of 5,204 adults discharged after acute heart failure. The exposure was NT-proBNP at discharge; the pre-specified primary outcome was 30-day unplanned readmission, ascertained from the national registry. NT-proBNP was available for 5,065 of 5,204 participants (97.3%); the primary analysis was complete-case, with a pre-specified multiple-imputation sensitivity analysis. Associations were estimated by multivariable logistic regression adjusted for age, sex, LVEF, and NYHA class, selected as confounders on a pre-specified causal diagram. The study followed STROBE.

**Results.** The 30-day readmission rate was 12.8% (95% CI 11.9–13.7). Higher discharge NT-proBNP was independently associated with readmission (adjusted OR 1.25 per log-unit, 95% CI 1.14–1.38, p < 0.001), with the excess concentrated in the upper two quartiles. The association was unchanged in the multiple-imputation sensitivity analysis (OR 1.25, 95% CI 1.13–1.38).

**Discussion.** In this cohort, discharge NT-proBNP was independently associated with 30-day readmission, consistent with the physiology of persistent congestion. The estimate is an association, not a causal effect: residual confounding from unmeasured severity cannot be excluded, and the single-registry ascertainment misses readmissions to other systems. The findings are hypothesis-supporting and require external validation before they change discharge practice.

## How the paper was built

Every move above follows a rule from the book:

- The **title** names the exposure, outcome, and design ([article structure](02-article-structure.qmd), on titles), and the PICO question that generated it comes from the [framing chapter](framing-the-question.qmd).
- The **structured abstract** states the main finding with its effect size and confidence interval, not just a p-value ([article structure](02-article-structure.qmd), on abstracts; [presenting data](04-presenting-data.qmd), on reporting numbers).
- The **introduction** funnels from the field to one gap and ends on the question ([article structure](02-article-structure.qmd), on the hourglass).
- The **methods** name the primary outcome once, report the missing-data denominator and handling, and justify the covariates by a causal diagram rather than by availability ([reporting](06-reporting-guidelines.qmd), on STROBE item 12; [statistical writing](statistical-writing.qmd); [framing the research question](framing-the-question.qmd), on confounding).
- The **results** lead with the event rate, then the adjusted estimate with its interval, then the sensitivity check, in the order the methods promised ([statistical writing](statistical-writing.qmd), on the methods–results contract).
- The **discussion** answers the question in the first sentence, then bounds it: association not causation, named limitations, no overreach ([article structure](02-article-structure.qmd), on the discussion; [statistical writing](statistical-writing.qmd), on correlation and causation).

The figures for a cohort like this (a distribution of the biomarker, a Kaplan–Meier curve of readmission-free survival, a table of baseline characteristics) are built to the standards in Part II, and the whole analysis is seeded and version-controlled to the standards in Part III. One question, answered once, reported so a reader can check every number against the next: that is the whole book in four paragraphs.
